references.text: Isaiah describes how God does not hear the prayers of those who stretch out their hands in self-righteousness: 'When you spread out your hands in prayer, I hide my eyes from you' (Jes 1:15). The Pharisee's prayer was characterized by self-satisfaction rather than humility.

God warns against those who say, 'Keep away; do not come near me, for I am too holy for you!' (Isa 65:5). The Pharisee's attitude—that he is better than other people—reflects this self-righteous disposition that is like smoke in God's nostrils.

Proverbs speaks of a generation that 'is clean in its own eyes, yet is not washed from its filth' (Prov 30:12). The Pharisee's prayer reveals someone who considers themselves righteous without seeing their own need for forgiveness.

Boasting without good reason is compared to empty clouds: 'Like clouds and wind without rain is the one who boasts of gifts never given' (Prov 25:14). The Pharisee's self-praise before God was empty and lacked true piety.

Jesus says, 'You are those who justify yourselves in the sight of others, but God knows your hearts; for what is highly esteemed among men is an abomination in the sight of God' (Luke 16:15). The Pharisee's prayer is a clear example of this self-justification.

The introduction to the parable explains that it is directed at those 'who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and looked down on everyone else' (Luke 18:9). The Pharisee's prayer in verse 11 illustrates exactly this attitude.

Jesus concludes that the tax collector went home justified, not the Pharisee: 'For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted' (Luke 18:14). The Pharisee's self-exaltation in prayer led to his humiliation.

Paul writes about those who 'did not know God's righteousness, and sought to establish their own' (Rom 10:3). The Pharisee's prayer is a classic example of trying to establish one's own righteousness rather than submitting to God's.

Paul mentions his own background as a Pharisee and all external reasons to trust in the flesh, yet counts it as loss (Phil 3:4-6). This contrasts with the Pharisee's self-glorifying listing of his own merits.

The church in Laodicea says, 'I am rich; I have become wealthy and need nothing,' but does not know that they are 'wretched, pitiful, poor, blind, and naked' (Rev 3:17). The same spiritual blindness characterized the Pharisee's prayer, where he failed to see his own need.
